items.prompt: A public API must allow each API key 100 requests per minute and reply 429 to anything over the quota.
items.why: A per-key quota with immediate rejection is the definition of a rate limiter. A load balancer never refuses work.

items.prompt: Traffic is growing and a single API server is at 90% CPU even though every client is behaving normally.
items.why: The load is legitimate, so you need more capacity spread across servers, not fewer allowed requests. Add servers behind a load balancer.

items.prompt: Users upload videos in bursts at the top of every hour; every upload must eventually be transcoded, but the transcoders can only handle a steady rate.
items.why: 'Every job must eventually succeed' plus a bursty producer → buffer the work in a queue and let consumers drain it. Rejecting uploads would lose work.

items.prompt: Attackers are trying thousands of passwords per account against the login endpoint.
items.why: Abuse of an expensive or dangerous endpoint → limit per account and per IP (and fail closed if the counter store is down).

items.prompt: Your SMS provider allows at most 50 messages per second from your account; above that it drops them silently.
items.why: A fragile downstream with a hard throughput cap → throttle outbound calls to it (leaky or token bucket), usually behind a queue.

items.prompt: The same product page is requested 20 000 times per second and each request runs the same expensive database query.
items.why: Many identical reads from legitimate users → cache the result. Limiting would just turn real users away.

items.prompt: Free-tier customers may make 1 000 calls per day, paid ones 100 000; quotas must hold across 30 gateway nodes.
items.why: Per-tier quotas → rate limiting with counters in a shared store (atomic increments) so all 30 nodes see the same count.
